dx: Fat embolism syndrome after a femoral shaft fracture
case: A 23-year-old man is admitted after a motorcycle collision with a closed fracture of the right femoral shaft. The leg is splinted while he awaits surgical fixation. Thirty-six hours after the injury he becomes confused and short of breath. His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Petechiae are present over the upper chest, axillae, and conjunctivae. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.49 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 30 mm Hg (35 to 45), and PaO2 52 mm Hg (75 to 100). Platelet count is 96,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy opacities. The diagnosis is fat embolism syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why he has neurologic and skin findings in addition to lung injury?
options: Thrombus from a deep calf vein lodging in a pulmonary artery
Gas bubbles entering the venous system through torn veins
Immune complexes depositing in small vessel walls
Fat globules passing through lung capillaries to arteries
approach: Link the setting (long bone fracture, onset 24 to 72 hours later) to fat embolism.
Ask how material that enters veins can reach the brain and skin, which lie on the arterial side.
Small, deformable fat globules squeeze through pulmonary capillaries (or a patent foramen ovale) into systemic arteries.
questions.why: Fat from injured bone marrow enters torn marrow venules and travels to the lungs, where it lodges in capillaries. Lipase breaks the fat into free fatty acids that injure the alveolar capillary endothelium, so the lung picture resembles ARDS. Small globules deform and pass through the pulmonary capillary bed into the systemic circulation, where they block small vessels in the brain and skin. This produces the classic triad of hypoxemia, confusion, and a petechial rash over the upper body. Platelets stick to the fat and are consumed, which explains the thrombocytopenia.
whyNot: A deep vein thrombus is too large to cross the pulmonary capillaries, so it causes lung findings without petechiae. It would reach the brain only through a right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale.
Air embolism follows central venous catheter placement or diving decompression and has a sudden onset, without a delay of a day or more after a fracture.
Immune complex vasculitis produces palpable purpura over the legs and does not follow a fracture by 1 to 3 days.
Correct.

questions.stem: His blood gas was drawn at sea level (barometric pressure 760 mm Hg) while he breathed room air (FiO2 0.21). Assume a respiratory quotient of 0.8. Which of the following is closest to his alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient?
options: About 60 mm Hg
About 70 mm Hg
About 78 mm Hg
About 98 mm Hg
approach: Use the alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = 0.21 x (760 - 47) - 30/0.8 = 150 - 37.5, which is about 112 mm Hg.
Subtract the measured PaO2: 112 - 52 is about 60 mm Hg.
A normal gradient at age 23 is about 5 to 10 mm Hg, so his gradient is widened, pointing to a gas exchange defect in the lung.
questions.why: The alveolar gas equation estimates the oxygen pressure in the alveoli. Inspired PO2 is FiO2 times (barometric pressure minus water vapor pressure of 47 mm Hg). Alveolar PO2 is inspired PO2 minus PaCO2 divided by the respiratory quotient. The A-a gradient is PAO2 minus PaO2. A normal gradient with hypoxemia means low inspired oxygen or hypoventilation. A widened gradient, as here, means the lung itself is failing to transfer oxygen, from V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion limitation. Fat emboli and the chemical injury they cause produce both dead space and shunt.
whyNot: Correct.
About 70 mm Hg results from forgetting to subtract water vapor pressure (0.21 x 760 is about 160).
About 78 mm Hg results from forgetting both water vapor pressure and the division of PaCO2 by 0.8.
About 98 mm Hg results from ignoring the PaCO2 term, as if alveolar CO2 took up no space.

questions.stem: While breathing spontaneously, his tidal volume is 400 mL, his PaCO2 is 30 mm Hg, and the PCO2 of his mixed expired gas is 15 mm Hg. Which of the following is closest to his physiologic dead space?
options: 100 mL
150 mL
200 mL
400 mL
approach: Use the Bohr equation with PaCO2 standing in for alveolar PCO2: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2)/PaCO2.
(30 - 15)/30 = 0.5, so dead space is 0.5 x 400 mL = 200 mL.
Normal VD/VT is about 0.3, so fat emboli have added alveolar dead space to the anatomic dead space of about 150 mL.
questions.why: Physiologic dead space is anatomic dead space plus alveolar dead space, which is alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused. Fat globules blocking pulmonary capillaries create alveolar dead space. Expired CO2 is diluted by gas from these unperfused units, so mixed expired PCO2 falls well below PaCO2. Alveolar ventilation equals (tidal volume minus dead space) times rate. At 30 breaths/min his minute ventilation is 12 L/min, but only half of each breath reaches perfused alveoli. Rapid shallow breathing makes this worse, because dead space stays fixed while each breath gets smaller.
whyNot: 100 mL is less than the normal anatomic dead space of about 150 mL, so it cannot be his total physiologic dead space.
150 mL is the normal anatomic dead space. It ignores the alveolar dead space created by the emboli.
Correct.
400 mL results from dividing by mixed expired PCO2 instead of PaCO2. It would mean that no gas from any breath reached perfused alveoli.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most distal airway in which no gas exchange occurs, marking the end of his anatomic dead space?
options: Segmental bronchus
Terminal bronchiole
Respiratory bronchiole
Alveolar duct
approach: The conducting zone moves air but has no alveoli, so it forms the anatomic dead space.
The respiratory zone begins where alveoli first bud from the airway wall, at the respiratory bronchioles.
The last purely conducting airway is the terminal bronchiole. The fat emboli add alveolar dead space beyond this point, in alveoli that lose their blood flow.
questions.why: The conducting zone runs from the nose and trachea through the bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles. It warms, humidifies, and filters air but has no alveoli, so its volume, about 150 mL in an adult, is the anatomic dead space. The respiratory zone starts at the respiratory bronchioles, whose walls carry scattered alveoli, and continues through alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs. Airway resistance is greatest in the medium-sized bronchi, because the many small airways are arranged in parallel and have a huge total cross-sectional area.
whyNot: Segmental bronchi are conducting airways, but many more generations of conducting airways lie beyond them before gas exchange begins.
Correct.
Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli budding from their walls, so they are the first site of gas exchange and belong to the respiratory zone.
Alveolar ducts are lined almost entirely by alveolar openings and are part of the respiratory zone.

dx: Parapneumonic empyema complicating pneumococcal lobar pneumonia
case: A 61-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever and sharp right-sided chest pain for 4 days. Nine days ago she was diagnosed with right lower lobe pneumonia and started oral antibiotics. A pneumococcal urinary antigen test was positive. She has never received a pneumococcal vaccine. Her temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. There is dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds at the right base. Chest CT shows a loculated right pleural fluid collection with enhancing pleura. Thoracentesis yields thick, cloudy yellow fluid with pH 6.9 (normal pleural fluid about 7.6), glucose 28 mg/dL (serum 110 mg/dL), and LDH 2,600 U/L. Gram stain shows neutrophils and gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. The diagnosis is parapneumonic empyema.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of findings was most likely present over the right lower lobe at her original diagnosis, before fluid collected in the pleural space?
options: Dullness, decreased fremitus, and absent breath sounds
Hyperresonance, decreased fremitus, and absent breath sounds
Dullness, increased fremitus, and egophony
Resonance, normal fremitus, and diffuse wheezes
approach: Pneumococcal lobar pneumonia fills the alveoli of a whole lobe with exudate (consolidation).
Solid lung transmits vibration and sound better than air-filled lung, while fluid in the pleural space blocks them.
Consolidation therefore gives dullness with increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, and egophony.
questions.why: Lobar pneumonia moves through four stages: congestion, red hepatization (alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin), gray hepatization (red cells break down, fibrin and neutrophils remain), and resolution. The airless, liver-like lobe is dull to percussion, but because the airways stay open and the tissue is solid, voice sounds and fremitus are transmitted more strongly. Bronchopneumonia, typical of Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae, is patchy and centered on bronchioles, so the signs are less focal. Her current findings of dullness with decreased breath sounds reflect the pleural fluid that came later.
whyNot: Dullness with decreased fremitus and absent breath sounds is the pattern of a pleural effusion, which describes her now, not at diagnosis.
Hyperresonance with decreased fremitus and absent breath sounds is the pattern of a pneumothorax.
Correct.
Normal resonance with diffuse wheezes fits bronchospasm, as in asthma, with no consolidation.

topics: Physical signs of consolidation and effusion

questions.stem: Which of the following components of the organism seen on Gram stain is the main reason it resists ingestion by neutrophils and alveolar macrophages in a host without specific antibody?
options: Cytolytic pneumolysin toxin
Polysaccharide capsule
Secreted IgA protease
Cell wall lipoteichoic acid
approach: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci in lobar pneumonia point to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Resistance to phagocytosis depends on blocking opsonization and contact with phagocyte receptors.
The polysaccharide capsule does this, and antibody against it (from infection or vaccination) is what overcomes it.
questions.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble gram-positive diplococcus and the most common cause of community-acquired and lobar pneumonia. Its polysaccharide capsule is its key virulence factor. The capsule hides surface C3b and the bacterial wall, so phagocytes cannot grip it, and unencapsulated strains are largely avirulent. Opsonizing IgG against capsular polysaccharide restores phagocytosis, which is why vaccines target the capsule. Splenic macrophages clear opsonized encapsulated organisms, so asplenic patients are at high risk of overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis.
whyNot: Pneumolysin damages host cell membranes and cilia and promotes tissue injury, but it is not what prevents phagocytosis.
Correct.
IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA, helping the organism colonize the nasopharynx. It does not block phagocytosis in the alveoli.
Lipoteichoic acid triggers inflammation through Toll-like receptor 2 and helps adhesion. It does not prevent ingestion.

questions.stem: Her chest pain is sharp, worsens with each breath, and is felt over the lower lateral chest wall on the right. Which of the following nerves carries this pain?
options: Lower intercostal nerves
Right phrenic nerve
Right vagus nerve
Thoracic sympathetic trunk
approach: Pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura, which has somatic sensory nerves. The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and does not sense pain.
The costal parietal pleura and the peripheral diaphragmatic pleura are supplied by the intercostal nerves.
Pain from these regions is felt sharply over the overlying chest wall, as in this patient.
questions.why: Inflammation of the parietal pleura causes sharp, well-localized pain that worsens with breathing. The costal pleura and the outer rim of the diaphragmatic pleura are supplied by intercostal nerves, so pain is felt over the chest wall (and sometimes the abdominal wall from the lower intercostal nerves). The mediastinal pleura and the central diaphragmatic pleura are supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so irritation there is referred to the shoulder. The visceral pleura receives autonomic fibers and is insensitive to pain, so lung disease is painless until it reaches the parietal pleura.
whyNot: Correct.
The phrenic nerve supplies the central diaphragmatic and mediastinal pleura. Irritation there causes pain referred to the shoulder, not the lateral chest wall.
The vagus nerve carries autonomic fibers to the lungs and visceral pleura, which do not give sharp localized pain.
The sympathetic trunk supplies the visceral pleura and lung, which are insensitive to the pain of pleurisy.

questions.stem: A pneumococcal conjugate vaccine couples capsular polysaccharides to a protein carrier. Which of the following best explains why conjugation produces long-lasting, boostable immunity that plain polysaccharide vaccines give poorly?
options: Repeating sugar units cross-linking B cell receptors
Polysaccharide presented on MHC class II to helper T cells
Polysaccharide presented on MHC class I to cytotoxic T cells
Carrier peptides presented by B cells to helper T cells
approach: Plain polysaccharides are T-cell independent antigens: they cross-link B cell receptors but cannot be presented on MHC to T cells.
In a conjugate, a B cell that recognizes the polysaccharide takes up the whole molecule and presents carrier peptides on MHC class II.
Carrier-specific helper T cells then give the B cell CD40 ligand and cytokines, driving class switching, affinity maturation, and memory.
questions.why: T-cell independent responses to plain polysaccharide produce mostly IgM, little memory, and no booster effect, and they work poorly in children under 2 years. Conjugation links the polysaccharide to a protein such as a diphtheria toxoid variant. The polysaccharide-specific B cell internalizes the conjugate, digests the protein, and shows carrier peptides to CD4+ helper T cells. The linked T cell help turns on class switching to IgG, germinal center affinity maturation, and memory B cells against the polysaccharide. The same principle underlies the Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine.
whyNot: Cross-linking of B cell receptors by repeating sugar units is the T-cell independent response to plain polysaccharide, which gives weak memory.
Polysaccharides are not loaded onto MHC class II. MHC molecules present peptides.
MHC class I presents peptides made inside the cell to CD8+ T cells. It does not present polysaccharides or drive antibody responses.
Correct.

dx: Pulmonary blastomycosis with skin dissemination in a healthy outdoorsman
case: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of cough, fevers, night sweats, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss over 2 months. He lives in northern Wisconsin and spends weekends hunting and canoeing along wooded riverbanks. He takes no medications, and an HIV test is negative. His temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. A 3-cm crusted, warty plaque with a raised border is present on the left cheek. Chest x-ray shows a mass-like consolidation in the right upper lobe. Biopsy of the skin lesion shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and mixed neutrophilic and granulomatous inflammation containing yeast forms. The diagnosis is pulmonary blastomycosis with cutaneous dissemination.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of the yeast forms in the biopsy specimen most specifically identifies this organism?
options: Tiny oval yeasts crowded inside macrophage cytoplasm
Large thick-walled spherules full of endospores
Thick-walled yeasts with one broad-based bud
Large yeasts with many narrow-based peripheral buds
approach: The Great Lakes region, outdoor exposure near rivers, and warty skin lesions point to Blastomyces dermatitidis.
Each dimorphic fungus has a distinctive tissue form at body temperature.
Blastomyces appears as large thick-walled yeasts with a single broad-based bud.
questions.why: The endemic dimorphic fungi grow as molds in the environment and convert to tissue forms at body temperature after spores are inhaled. Blastomyces lives in moist soil and decaying wood around the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi River basins. In tissue it forms large (about 8 to 15 micrometers) yeasts with a thick, refractile wall and a single broad-based bud. Histoplasma, from bird and bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, forms tiny yeasts inside macrophages. Coccidioides, from desert soil in the southwestern United States, forms spherules filled with endospores.
whyNot: Tiny oval yeasts packed inside macrophages are Histoplasma capsulatum, linked to bird and bat droppings in caves and old buildings.
Spherules filled with endospores are Coccidioides immitis, found in the desert Southwest and California.
Correct.
Large yeasts with many narrow-based buds around the edge (a ship's wheel pattern) are Paracoccidioides, found in Latin America.

questions.stem: Besides the skin, which of the following sites is most commonly involved when this infection disseminates?
options: Vertebrae and long bones
Adrenal glands bilaterally
Meninges at the brain base
Mitral and aortic valves
approach: Endemic fungal pneumonia can spread through the blood even in healthy hosts.
Each endemic fungus has favored sites of spread.
Blastomycosis spreads most often to skin, then bone, then the male genitourinary tract (prostate, epididymis).
questions.why: Most endemic fungal infections in healthy people are mild or silent and heal with granulomas that can calcify and mimic tuberculosis on x-ray. Blastomycosis more often causes symptomatic pneumonia and a mass-like lesion that can be mistaken for lung cancer. When it disseminates, it favors the skin (warty or ulcerated lesions), bone (osteomyelitis, often vertebrae, ribs, and long bones), and the prostate and epididymis. Histoplasmosis disseminates mainly in people with weak cell-mediated immunity, to the reticuloendothelial system, adrenals, and oral mucosa. Coccidioidomycosis spreads to skin, bone, and the meninges.
whyNot: Correct.
Adrenal involvement with adrenal insufficiency is typical of disseminated histoplasmosis and tuberculosis.
Basilar meningitis is the dreaded complication of disseminated coccidioidomycosis and is uncommon in blastomycosis.
Fungal endocarditis is usually caused by Candida or Aspergillus in people who inject drugs or have prosthetic valves.

questions.stem: Inhaled conidia reach his alveoli and convert to yeast. The resident cell that first ingests them in the alveolar lumen has which of the following other normal functions?
options: Forming the thin barrier for gas diffusion
Clearing inhaled dust and used surfactant
Secreting surfactant and renewing type I cells
Detoxifying inhaled toxins with cytochrome P450
approach: The first phagocyte in the alveolar lumen is the alveolar macrophage.
Alveolar macrophages clear particles (dust cells), take up and break down used surfactant, and start inflammation by releasing cytokines.
Match that cell to its function among the options.
questions.why: Alveolar macrophages arise from fetal monocytes and renew themselves in the alveoli, with help from circulating monocytes during injury. They patrol the alveolar surface, ingest inhaled particles and microbes, and catabolize surfactant. Their development depends on GM-CSF, and loss of this signaling causes pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. Type I pneumocytes cover about 95% of the alveolar surface and form the thin gas exchange barrier. Type II pneumocytes make surfactant and divide to replace type I cells. Club cells in bronchioles secrete protective proteins, detoxify chemicals with cytochrome P450, and act as progenitor cells.
whyNot: Forming the thin gas exchange barrier is the job of type I pneumocytes, which are not phagocytic.
Correct.
Secreting surfactant and regenerating type I cells is the job of type II pneumocytes.
Cytochrome P450 detoxification is a function of club cells in the terminal bronchioles.

questions.stem: On room air his arterial blood gas shows PaO2 58 mm Hg (75 to 100) and PaCO2 34 mm Hg (35 to 45). After 20 minutes on 100% oxygen, his PaO2 rises only to 110 mm Hg. Which of the following is the main mechanism of his hypoxemia?
options: Alveolar hypoventilation
Diffusion limitation
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Intrapulmonary shunt
approach: His PaCO2 is low, so hypoventilation is excluded, and the A-a gradient is widened.
On 100% oxygen, V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation correct almost fully, with PaO2 rising to several hundred mm Hg.
A poor rise means blood is passing through alveoli that receive no ventilation, here the consolidated lobe.
questions.why: There are five causes of hypoxemia. Low inspired oxygen and hypoventilation keep a normal A-a gradient. Diffusion limitation, V/Q mismatch, and right-to-left shunt widen it. Breathing 100% oxygen raises PAO2 even in poorly ventilated units, so V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation correct well. In a shunt, blood flows past alveoli filled with exudate or collapsed, so it never meets the added oxygen, and mixing with that blood keeps PaO2 low. A consolidated lobe still perfused acts as an intrapulmonary shunt, partly reduced by hypoxic vasoconstriction.
whyNot: Hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and leaves a normal A-a gradient. His PaCO2 is low.
Diffusion limitation, as in interstitial fibrosis, worsens with exercise and corrects readily with supplemental oxygen.
V/Q mismatch, as in COPD or asthma, widens the gradient but corrects well with 100% oxygen because low V/Q units still receive some ventilation.
Correct.

dx: Ventilator-associated Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia in an intubated trauma patient
case: A 29-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit after a motorcycle collision with a closed head injury and rib fractures. She is intubated and mechanically ventilated. On hospital day 6 her temperature is 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 22/min on the ventilator, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Suctioning produces copious purulent secretions, and higher inspired oxygen is needed. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate in the right lower lobe. Gram stain of an endotracheal aspirate shows many neutrophils and gram-negative rods. The diagnosis is ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: Before culture results are available, which of the following pairs of organisms are the most likely causes of her pneumonia?
options: Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and MRSA
Legionella pneumophila and Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Fusobacterium and other oral anaerobes
approach: Pneumonia that starts 48 hours or more after intubation is ventilator-associated.
Late onset (day 5 or later) shifts the likely organisms toward multidrug-resistant hospital flora.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and MRSA lead that list, with enteric gram-negative rods and Acinetobacter.
questions.why: The endotracheal tube bypasses cough and mucociliary defenses, and colonized oropharyngeal secretions pool above the cuff and leak into the lower airways. Within days, the oropharynx is colonized by hospital organisms. Early ventilator-associated pneumonia (first 4 days) is often caused by community organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Late-onset pneumonia, prior antibiotics, and long hospital stays favor Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Acinetobacter. Chemical aspiration pneumonitis is a different process: sterile acid injury within hours of aspiration.
whyNot: Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae cause community-acquired pneumonia and early ventilator-associated pneumonia, before hospital flora take over.
Correct.

Legionella and Mycoplasma cause atypical community-acquired pneumonia. Legionella can cause hospital outbreaks from contaminated water, but it is not a leading cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia.
Oral anaerobes cause aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess in people with impaired consciousness and poor dentition, usually acquired outside the ICU.

questions.stem: Culture of the aspirate grows non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar that are oxidase positive. Which of the following additional findings most strongly supports the most likely organism?
options: Growth only with added factors X and V
Mucoid colonies that ferment lactose
Growth only on buffered charcoal yeast agar
Blue-green pigment and a grapelike odor
approach: Growth on MacConkey agar as a non-lactose fermenter that is oxidase positive fits Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Pseudomonas makes pyocyanin and pyoverdine pigments and has a sweet grapelike odor.
Compare each option with the lab findings already given.
questions.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. It thrives in moist hospital settings and is a classic cause of pneumonia in ventilated patients and in cystic fibrosis. It produces blue-green pigments and a grapelike odor, and its exotoxin A inactivates elongation factor 2. Haemophilus influenzae needs factors X (hemin) and V (NAD) and grows on chocolate agar. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative rod with a thick mucoid capsule, seen in alcohol use disorder. Legionella needs buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron and does not grow on MacConkey agar.
whyNot: Dependence on factors X and V describes Haemophilus influenzae, which does not grow on MacConkey agar.
Mucoid lactose-fermenting colonies describe Klebsiella pneumoniae, which is also oxidase negative.
Legionella grows only on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, so it would not form colonies on MacConkey agar.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomic features best explains why aspirated secretions and a too deeply placed endotracheal tube both tend to enter the right lung?
options: Larger volume of the three-lobed right lung
Horizontal fissure directing air to the middle lobe
Wider, more vertical right main bronchus
Cardiac notch compressing the left main bronchus
approach: Material moving down the trachea follows the straightest and widest path.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more in line with the trachea than the left.
So both aspirated material and an advanced tube favor the right side, and gravity decides the segment.
questions.why: The left main bronchus is longer and leaves the trachea at a sharper angle because it must pass under the aortic arch and in front of the esophagus to reach the left hilum. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical. The right lung has three lobes separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures. The left has two lobes, an oblique fissure, a lingula, and a cardiac notch. When a person is upright, aspirated material tends to reach the right lower lobe basal segments. When supine, it reaches the superior segment of the right lower lobe or the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
whyNot: The right lung is somewhat larger, but lung volume does not decide which bronchus a falling bolus enters.
The horizontal fissure separates the right upper and middle lobes. It does not direct airflow or aspirated material.
Correct.
The cardiac notch is an indentation in the anterior border of the left upper lobe. It does not compress the left main bronchus.

questions.stem: On day 7 her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.10 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 60 mm Hg (35 to 45), and HCO3- 18 mEq/L (22 to 28). Which of the following best describes her acid-base status?
options: Respiratory acidosis with a coexisting metabolic acidosis
Acute respiratory acidosis with expected compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with expected compensation
Metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
approach: A low pH with a high PaCO2 means a primary respiratory acidosis.
Acute compensation raises HCO3- about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2, so the expected value is about 26 mEq/L, and chronic compensation would give about 31 to 32 mEq/L.
Her HCO3- of 18 is far below either, so a second, metabolic acidosis is present, most likely lactic acidosis from sepsis.
questions.why: Primary respiratory disorders change PaCO2, and the kidneys compensate by changing bicarbonate. In acute respiratory acidosis, buffering raises HCO3- about 1 mEq/L for every 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2. Over 3 to 5 days, renal acid excretion and bicarbonate generation raise it 3 to 4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg. In acute respiratory alkalosis HCO3- falls about 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg, and in chronic alkalosis about 4 to 5. When the bicarbonate falls outside the expected range, a second disorder is present. Here the low HCO3- with a high PaCO2 moves the pH in the same direction, giving severe acidemia.
whyNot: Correct.
Acute respiratory acidosis alone would give HCO3- of about 26 mEq/L, and her value of 18 is far too low.
Chronic respiratory acidosis would give HCO3- of about 31 to 32 mEq/L and a pH close to normal.
Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis lowers PaCO2. Her PaCO2 is high, so her lungs are adding to the acidosis.

dx: Primary pulmonary tuberculosis with a Ghon complex in a child
case: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of mild cough and low-grade fevers for 3 weeks. Her grandfather, who lives with the family, was recently diagnosed with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis. She has not traveled. Her temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A tuberculin skin test shows 14 mm of induration at 48 hours. Chest x-ray shows a small subpleural opacity in the right lower lobe and an enlarged right hilar lymph node. An HIV test is negative. The diagnosis is primary pulmonary tuberculosis with a Ghon complex.

questions.stem: Her infection is contained and she remains well. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on a chest x-ray 5 years later?
options: Apical cavity with surrounding fibrosis
Innumerable 2-mm nodules in both lungs
Calcified lower lobe nodule and hilar node
Bilateral hilar nodes with clear lung fields
approach: Primary tuberculosis seeds a subpleural focus in the lower or middle lung zones and drains to hilar nodes, forming the Ghon complex.
In most immunocompetent hosts, cell-mediated immunity walls off both sites in caseating granulomas.
These heal by fibrosis and calcification, leaving a calcified Ghon complex (Ranke complex) while bacilli may remain dormant.
questions.why: Inhaled bacilli usually settle in the well-ventilated lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, close to the pleura (the Ghon focus). They travel to hilar nodes, and the focus plus the nodes is the Ghon complex. After 3 to 8 weeks, Th1 immunity develops, the tuberculin test turns positive, and caseating granulomas contain the infection. The lesions fibrose and calcify, and the person has latent infection with a positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay. Induration of 5 mm or more is positive in a close contact of an active case, so her 14 mm result is clearly positive.
whyNot: An apical cavity with fibrosis is secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis, which arises in the high-oxygen lung apex years later in some infected people.
Innumerable tiny nodules are miliary tuberculosis from bloodstream spread, a feature of progressive disease in young children or the immunocompromised.
Correct.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lungs is the classic x-ray pattern of sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: A Ziehl-Neelsen stain of an early-morning gastric aspirate shows slender rods that keep the red carbolfuchsin dye after an acid-alcohol wash. Which of the following cell wall components accounts for this staining property?
options: Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids
Long-chain mycolic acids
Lipopolysaccharide outer membrane
Polysaccharide capsule
approach: Young children swallow their sputum, so gastric aspirate is used to find bacilli.
Holding the dye after acid-alcohol is the definition of acid-fast staining.
Acid fastness comes from the waxy mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell envelope.
questions.why: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing, obligate aerobic rod with a lipid-rich cell envelope. Long-chain mycolic acids make the wall waxy and hard to stain, but once carbolfuchsin is driven in with heat, acid-alcohol cannot remove it. The wall also contains cord factor (trehalose dimycolate), which inhibits neutrophil migration and stimulates TNF-alpha release, and sulfatides, which help block phagosome-lysosome fusion. The organism spreads in airborne droplet nuclei small enough to reach the alveoli. Its thick lipid wall also explains resistance to drying and to many disinfectants.
whyNot: Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids defines gram-positive bacteria. Mycobacteria stain poorly with Gram stain.
Correct.
Lipopolysaccharide in an outer membrane defines gram-negative bacteria. Mycobacteria have no lipopolysaccharide outer membrane.
A polysaccharide capsule protects organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae from phagocytosis. It does not cause acid-fast staining.

questions.stem: Six years later she develops juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and a TNF-alpha inhibitor is considered. Which of the following best explains why her latent infection could reactivate on this therapy?
options: TNF-alpha drives IgE class switching in B cells
TNF-alpha stimulates opsonizing IgG production
TNF-alpha recruits eosinophils that kill bacilli
TNF-alpha keeps granulomas walled off
approach: Containment of tuberculosis depends on granulomas.
Th1 cells release IFN-gamma to activate macrophages, and macrophages release TNF-alpha to recruit cells and hold the granuloma together.
Blocking TNF-alpha lets granulomas break down and dormant bacilli grow, so latent infection must be treated before therapy.
questions.why: Macrophages that ingest Mycobacterium tuberculosis present antigen and release IL-12, which drives naive CD4+ T cells to become Th1 cells. Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill bacilli and to form epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells. TNF-alpha from activated macrophages recruits monocytes and maintains the structure of the granuloma. Caseous necrosis forms in the center. TNF-alpha blockade, HIV infection, and other defects of this pathway allow reactivation and dissemination. People with defects in IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptors have severe mycobacterial infections.
whyNot: IgE class switching is driven by IL-4 from Th2 cells and plays no protective role against mycobacteria.
Antibody contributes little to defense against intracellular mycobacteria. Control depends on cell-mediated immunity.
Eosinophils defend mainly against helminths. They do not kill mycobacteria.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her enlarged lymph node lies at the right lung hilum. Which of the following structures in the root of the right lung normally lies superior to the right pulmonary artery?
options: Upper lobe bronchus
Superior pulmonary vein
Inferior pulmonary vein
Bronchus intermedius
approach: Recall the arrangement of each lung root from the medial view.
On the right, the upper lobe bronchus branches off before the hilum and lies above the pulmonary artery (the eparterial bronchus).
The pulmonary veins lie anterior and inferior, and the bronchus intermedius continues below and behind the artery.
questions.why: At each hilum the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and most inferior structures. On the left, the pulmonary artery is the highest structure, lying above the left main bronchus. On the right, the upper lobe bronchus leaves the main bronchus outside the lung and lies above the pulmonary artery, which crosses in front of the bronchus. Bronchopulmonary and hilar lymph nodes cluster around these structures. Enlarged hilar nodes in primary tuberculosis can compress a bronchus, especially the right middle lobe bronchus in children, causing collapse.
whyNot: Correct.
The superior pulmonary vein lies anterior and below the pulmonary artery at the hilum.
The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure in the lung root.
The bronchus intermedius continues downward after the upper lobe bronchus branches, so it lies below the level of the artery's entry.

dx: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurrent epistaxis and a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation causing paradoxical embolic stroke
case: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sudden weakness of his left arm and leg. He has had frequent nosebleeds since childhood, and his father had the same problem. His temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Small red blanching macules are present on the lips, tongue, and fingertips, and there is digital clubbing. Hemoglobin is 18.1 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5). MRI of the brain shows an acute infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory. Chest CT shows a 3-cm vascular lesion in the right lower lobe with one feeding artery and one draining vein. On echocardiography with agitated saline, bubbles appear in the left atrium after several cardiac cycles. The diagnosis is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation and paradoxical embolic stroke.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely source of the embolus that caused his stroke?
options: Thrombus in a fibrillating left atrium
Venous thrombus crossing the malformation
Plaque rupture in the right internal carotid
Bleeding from a cerebral telangiectasia
approach: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation connects a pulmonary artery directly to a pulmonary vein with no capillary bed.
The lung capillaries normally filter small venous clots and bacteria from the blood.
Without that filter, a venous clot passes straight to the left heart and the brain, a paradoxical embolus.
questions.why: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is autosomal dominant and is caused most often by mutations in endoglin or ALK1, which disrupt TGF-beta family signaling in endothelial cells. Vessels form fragile direct artery-to-vein connections: telangiectasias in the skin and mucosa and larger arteriovenous malformations in the lungs, brain, and liver. A pulmonary malformation is a right-to-left shunt, so it causes hypoxemia that does not correct with oxygen, secondary polycythemia, and clubbing, and it can rupture to cause hemoptysis. Loss of capillary filtering allows paradoxical emboli (stroke) and brain abscess. Bubbles reaching the left atrium after a delay of several beats point to an intrapulmonary shunt, while bubbles within 1 to 3 beats suggest an intracardiac shunt.
whyNot: Atrial fibrillation causes cardioembolic stroke, but nothing in his history points to it, and his lung lesion offers a direct route for venous emboli.
Correct.
Carotid plaque rupture causes strokes mainly in older people with atherosclerotic risk factors, and it does not explain his shunt.
His MRI shows an infarct, which is ischemic. Bleeding from a vascular lesion would cause a hemorrhagic stroke.

questions.stem: Years later he has a brisk nosebleed that comes from the back of the nasal cavity and does not stop with anterior packing. Which of the following arteries is the most likely source?
options: Anterior ethmoidal artery
Superior labial artery
Sphenopalatine artery
Greater palatine artery
approach: Most nosebleeds arise anteriorly in Kiesselbach area, where four arteries meet on the septum.
Bleeding high and far back that fails anterior packing is posterior epistaxis.
Posterior epistaxis comes from branches of the sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery.
questions.why: Kiesselbach area on the anterior nasal septum is where branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries join. This is the source of about 90% of nosebleeds, which are usually easy to control with pressure. Posterior epistaxis comes from the posterior lateral nasal and septal branches of the sphenopalatine artery. It is less common, tends to occur in older people and those with hypertension or bleeding tendency, can be heavy, and may need posterior packing or arterial ligation. In hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, fragile mucosal telangiectasias bleed again and again.
whyNot: The anterior ethmoidal artery, from the ophthalmic artery, supplies the anterior superior septum and joins Kiesselbach area. It is not the usual source of posterior bleeding.
The superior labial artery, from the facial artery, supplies the front of the septum near the nostril and contributes to anterior bleeds.
Correct.
The greater palatine artery reaches the anterior septum through the incisive canal and contributes to Kiesselbach area, not the posterior nasal cavity.

topics: Blood supply of the nasal cavity

questions.stem: At the time of his stroke, his PaO2 is 54 mm Hg (75 to 100) and his arterial oxygen saturation is 88%. Which of the following is closest to his arterial oxygen content?
options: 17.8 mL O2/dL
21.5 mL O2/dL
23.0 mL O2/dL
24.4 mL O2/dL
approach: Oxygen content = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2).
Bound oxygen: 1.34 x 18.1 x 0.88 is about 21.3 mL/dL. Dissolved oxygen: 0.003 x 54 is about 0.2 mL/dL.
Total is about 21.5 mL O2/dL, slightly above a normal value of about 20, because polycythemia offsets the low saturation.
questions.why: Almost all oxygen in blood is bound to hemoglobin, and each gram of fully saturated hemoglobin carries about 1.34 mL of oxygen. Dissolved oxygen adds only 0.003 mL/dL per mm Hg of PaO2. Chronic hypoxemia from his shunt stimulates erythropoietin, and the higher hemoglobin restores content despite low saturation. In anemia, PaO2 and saturation are normal but content falls. In carbon monoxide poisoning, PaO2 is normal but saturation and content fall. Polycythemia raises blood viscosity, which may add to thrombotic risk.
whyNot: 17.8 assumes a normal hemoglobin of 15 g/dL and misses his polycythemia.
Correct.
23.0 uses 0.03 instead of 0.003 for dissolved oxygen, overstating the dissolved part tenfold.
24.4 leaves out the saturation, as if all of his hemoglobin were carrying oxygen.

questions.stem: His malformation was closed by embolization. Five years later, after a long flight, he develops sudden dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. CT angiography shows emboli in segmental branches of both pulmonary arteries. Reference ranges are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg, and PaO2 75 to 100 mm Hg. Which of the following arterial blood gas patterns is most likely?
options: pH 7.30, PaCO2 52 mm Hg, PaO2 60 mm Hg
pH 7.32, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, PaO2 95 mm Hg
pH 7.40, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, PaO2 95 mm Hg
pH 7.49, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, PaO2 62 mm Hg
approach: Prolonged immobility on a long flight causes venous stasis, part of Virchow triad, and deep vein thrombosis.
Emboli block perfusion, creating dead space and V/Q mismatch, which lowers PaO2 and widens the A-a gradient.
Hypoxemia, pain, and stimulation of lung receptors drive hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 and causing respiratory alkalosis.
questions.why: Most pulmonary emboli come from deep veins of the legs. Virchow triad of stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability explains the risk. Typical findings are sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis and a widened A-a gradient. D-dimer is raised. A large saddle embolus can cause acute right heart strain and sudden death. PaCO2 rises only when the patient tires or the obstruction is massive enough to cause shock. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia does not cause clots; his embolism follows the flight.
whyNot: A low pH with a high PaCO2 is acute respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation, as in opioid overdose or late respiratory failure, not typical early pulmonary embolism.
A low pH with a low PaCO2 and normal PaO2 is metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, as in diabetic ketoacidosis.
A completely normal gas is possible with small emboli but is not the most likely pattern with bilateral segmental clots and symptoms.
Correct.

dx: HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the palatine tonsil
case: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painless lump on the left side of his neck for 2 months. He has never smoked and drinks one or two glasses of wine weekly. His temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. The left palatine tonsil is enlarged by a firm, 2-cm ulcerated mass. A 3-cm firm, nontender lymph node is palpable below the angle of the left mandible. Fine-needle aspiration of the node shows nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, and the tumor cells show strong diffuse p16 staining. In situ hybridization detects human papillomavirus type 16 DNA. The diagnosis is HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the palatine tonsil.

questions.stem: Compared with a squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue in a man who smokes and drinks heavily, his tumor is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Wild-type TP53 with p53 degraded by viral E6
Inactivating TP53 point mutations from tobacco carcinogens
Loss of p16 expression from CDKN2A gene deletion
Activating KRAS point mutation from tobacco smoke
approach: HPV-driven tumors use viral oncoproteins to switch off tumor suppressors, so they do not need mutations in those genes.
HPV E6 targets p53 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation, so the TP53 gene usually stays wild type.
Tobacco and alcohol related oral cancers instead accumulate TP53 mutations and CDKN2A (p16) loss.
questions.why: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma has two main causes. Tobacco and alcohol cause tumors throughout the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx, usually in older people, with keratinizing histology, TP53 mutations, and loss of p16. High-risk HPV, mainly type 16, causes tumors of the tonsils and base of tongue, often in younger people who do not smoke. Viral E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb, so p16 rises and serves as a marker. HPV-positive tumors are often small primaries that present with cystic neck nodes and respond better to treatment than tobacco-related tumors.
whyNot: Correct.
TP53 mutations from tobacco carcinogens are typical of tobacco and alcohol related head and neck cancer, not HPV-driven tumors.
Loss of p16 is common in tobacco-related tumors. HPV-positive tumors overexpress p16, as in this patient.
KRAS mutations are typical of lung adenocarcinoma in smokers and are uncommon in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: In his tumor cells, the HPV E7 protein binds the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein. Which of the following normal functions of hypophosphorylated Rb is lost?
options: Inducing p21 to inhibit cyclin-dependent kinases
Activating BAX to trigger mitochondrial apoptosis
Holding E2F transcription factors inactive in G1
Excising bulky DNA adducts by nucleotide excision
approach: Rb is the gatekeeper of the G1 to S transition.
In its hypophosphorylated form, Rb binds E2F and blocks transcription of genes needed for DNA synthesis.
E7 binding frees E2F, so cells enter S phase without growth signals.
questions.why: In normal cells, growth signals raise cyclin D, which activates CDK4 and CDK6. These kinases phosphorylate Rb, releasing E2F to turn on S-phase genes. p16 inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 and keeps Rb active. p53 responds to DNA damage by inducing p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes and holds cells in G1 for repair, and by triggering apoptosis through BAX if damage is severe. When E7 removes Rb, the loss of feedback causes p16 to build up, which is why strong p16 staining marks HPV-driven tumors. Tobacco carcinogens act differently, forming DNA adducts that cause mutations in TP53 and other genes.
whyNot: Inducing p21 is a function of p53, which is targeted by HPV E6, not E7.
Activating BAX to start apoptosis is a function of p53 after severe DNA damage.
Correct.
Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky adducts and thymine dimers. It is a separate DNA repair system, defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.

topics: Rb and the G1 to S checkpoint

questions.stem: Squamous cell carcinoma arising at which of the following sites must first pass through squamous metaplasia, because the normal surface epithelium there is not squamous?
options: True vocal fold
Vestibular fold
Palatine tonsil
Lateral tongue border
approach: Sites exposed to friction and swallowed food are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The true vocal folds, oropharynx, tonsils, and oral tongue all have this lining.
The vestibular (false) vocal folds are lined by respiratory epithelium, so carcinoma there needs squamous metaplasia first.
questions.why: Most of the respiratory tract is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Areas that face mechanical stress have nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium instead: the oropharynx, the laryngopharynx, the upper surface of the epiglottis, and the true vocal folds, which vibrate and touch each other during speech. The vestibular folds above them have respiratory epithelium. Chronic irritation such as smoking can convert respiratory epithelium to squamous epithelium (metaplasia), which can progress to dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is the main malignant tumor of the larynx and the oropharynx.
whyNot: The true vocal folds are normally lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, so carcinoma there arises from native squamous cells.
Correct.
The palatine tonsil surface and its crypts are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The oral tongue is covered by stratified squamous epithelium, partly keratinized over the papillae.

topics: Epithelium of the larynx and pharynx

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why squamous cell carcinoma confined to the true vocal fold is usually found earlier and spreads to cervical nodes later than his tumor?
options: Early dysphagia and rich glottic lymphatics
Early referred otalgia and rich glottic lymphatics
Early stridor and sparse glottic lymphatics
Early hoarseness and sparse glottic lymphatics
approach: Even a small lesion on the vibrating edge of the true vocal fold changes the voice.
The true vocal folds have very few lymphatic vessels compared with the supraglottis and the tonsil.
So glottic cancer causes hoarseness early and spreads to nodes late.
questions.why: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is strongly linked to smoking and alcohol. Glottic tumors are the most common and present early with persistent hoarseness, which is why hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks in a smoker should be examined. Supraglottic tumors and oropharyngeal tumors drain into rich lymphatic networks and often present with neck nodes. Benign vocal fold nodules form at the junction of the front and middle thirds of both folds from voice overuse. Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is caused by HPV types 6 and 11 acquired at birth and causes recurrent warty growths with hoarseness in children.
whyNot: Dysphagia is a feature of hypopharyngeal or large supraglottic tumors, and the glottis has few lymphatics.
Referred ear pain through the vagus nerve is a late sign of advanced tumors, and the glottis has few lymphatics.
Stridor appears only when a tumor is large enough to narrow the airway, so it is a late sign.
Correct.

dx: ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with a malignant pleural effusion
case: A 34-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough for 2 months. Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg. There is dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the lower half of the right hemithorax. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion and a 3-cm peripheral mass in the right upper lobe. Thoracentesis yields 1.5 L of blood-tinged fluid. Cytology shows malignant cells forming glandular clusters. Molecular testing of the tumor cells shows an EML4-ALK gene fusion. The diagnosis is ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma with a malignant pleural effusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following genetic events most likely produced the EML4-ALK fusion in her tumor cells?
options: Point mutation in the ALK kinase domain
Inversion within the short arm of chromosome 2
Reciprocal translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22
Amplification of ALK in double minute chromosomes
approach: A fusion gene joins parts of two genes, so it comes from a chromosomal rearrangement, not a point mutation or amplification.
EML4 and ALK both lie on the short arm of chromosome 2 in opposite orientations.
A small inversion joins the 5' end of EML4 to the kinase domain of ALK.
questions.why: In the EML4-ALK fusion, the coiled-coil domain of EML4 makes the fusion protein dimerize without any ligand, so the ALK tyrosine kinase is always active. This drives growth through RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT, and JAK-STAT signaling. ALK rearrangements occur in a small fraction of lung adenocarcinomas, mostly in younger never-smokers, and they rarely occur together with EGFR or KRAS mutations. EGFR mutations are also more common in never-smokers, women, and people of East Asian descent, while KRAS mutations are linked to smoking. Small cell carcinoma instead shows near-universal loss of TP53 and RB1.
whyNot: Point mutations activate EGFR and KRAS in adenocarcinoma, but a point mutation cannot fuse two genes together.
Correct.
The 9;22 translocation forms BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, not EML4-ALK.
Amplification raises the copy number of an intact gene, as with MYC in small cell carcinoma or ERBB2 in breast cancer. It does not create a fusion.

questions.stem: Pleural fluid protein is 4.6 g/dL with serum protein 7.0 g/dL. Pleural fluid LDH is 410 U/L with serum LDH 230 U/L (serum upper limit of normal 220 U/L). Which of the following best describes the fluid?
options: Transudate from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure
Transudate from low plasma oncotic pressure
Chylous effusion from thoracic duct obstruction
Exudate from leaky vessels and blocked lymphatics
approach: Apply Light criteria: protein ratio 4.6/7.0 is about 0.66 (above 0.5), and LDH ratio 410/230 is about 1.8 (above 0.6).
Pleural LDH of 410 is also above two thirds of the serum upper limit (about 147 U/L).
Meeting any one criterion makes the fluid an exudate, and in cancer it forms from leaky tumor-involved pleura and blocked lymphatic drainage.
questions.why: Transudates form when Starling forces change across intact capillaries, from high hydrostatic pressure (heart failure) or low oncotic pressure (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). They are low in protein and LDH. Exudates form when the pleura is inflamed or invaded, so capillaries leak protein and cells, or when lymphatic drainage is blocked. Causes include pneumonia, empyema, cancer, tuberculosis, and pulmonary embolism. A bloody exudate suggests cancer, trauma, or pulmonary infarction. Lung and breast cancer are the most common causes of malignant pleural effusion.
whyNot: Raised hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure, gives a transudate with protein ratio below 0.5 and low LDH.
Low oncotic pressure, as in cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome, gives a transudate with low protein and LDH.
A chylous effusion is milky with triglycerides above about 110 mg/dL, from thoracic duct injury or obstruction, as in lymphoma. Her fluid is blood-tinged.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her tumor cells express high levels of PD-L1. Which of the following best explains how this helps the tumor escape immune killing?
options: Lowering MHC class I to escape natural killer cells
Binding CTLA-4 to block B7 costimulation of T cells
Binding PD-1 to inhibit tumor-specific CD8+ T cells
Shedding MHC class II to escape cytotoxic T cells
approach: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize tumor peptides on MHC class I and kill tumor cells.
Activated T cells express PD-1, an inhibitory checkpoint receptor.
Tumor PD-L1 engages PD-1 and turns off T cell signaling, causing T cell exhaustion within the tumor.
questions.why: Tumors evade immunity in several ways. They can lower MHC class I so cytotoxic T cells cannot see their antigens, though this makes them targets for natural killer cells, which kill cells missing MHC class I. They can express PD-L1, which binds PD-1 on T cells and suppresses their proliferation and killing. They can also recruit regulatory T cells and release immunosuppressive cytokines such as TGF-beta. Antibodies that block PD-1 or PD-L1 restore T cell attack. Lung cancers also share antigens with neurons, so the immune response can cause paraneoplastic syndromes such as anti-Hu encephalomyelitis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot: Lowering MHC class I helps a tumor hide from cytotoxic T cells but makes it more visible to natural killer cells.
CTLA-4 is a T cell receptor that binds B7 on antigen-presenting cells. PD-L1 does not bind CTLA-4.
Correct.
Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize antigen on MHC class I. Most tumor cells do not express MHC class II.

questions.stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical results on the pleural fluid cells best distinguishes her metastatic adenocarcinoma from malignant mesothelioma?
options: Positive TTF-1 and mucin stains
Positive calretinin and WT1 stains
Positive chromogranin and synaptophysin
Positive p40 and cytokeratin 5/6
approach: Lung adenocarcinoma is a gland-forming tumor that makes mucin and arises from peripheral airway and alveolar epithelium.
Thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) marks lung adenocarcinoma and small cell carcinoma.
Mesothelioma cells lack mucin and TTF-1 and instead stain for calretinin and WT1.
questions.why: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall and the most common in never-smokers and women. It is usually peripheral, forms glands, and makes mucin, and it often spreads to the pleura. Adenocarcinoma in situ grows along intact alveolar walls (lepidic growth) without invasion. Squamous cell carcinoma is usually central, forms keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, and stains for p40. Small cell carcinoma is central, has neuroendocrine markers, and is strongly linked to smoking. Mesothelioma, linked to asbestos, encases the lung in a pleural rind and stains for calretinin and WT1.
whyNot: Correct.
Calretinin and WT1 mark mesothelial cells and mesothelioma.
Chromogranin and synaptophysin mark neuroendocrine tumors such as small cell carcinoma and carcinoid.
p40 and cytokeratin 5/6 mark squamous cell carcinoma. Cytokeratin 5/6 is also positive in mesothelioma.

topics: Immunostains in lung and pleural tumors

dx: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome with coexisting obstructive sleep apnea
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and leg swelling for 6 months. Her husband reports loud snoring and pauses in her breathing during sleep. Her BMI is 44 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. She has bilateral pitting edema of the legs. Oxygen saturation is 87% on room air. Arterial blood gas while awake on room air shows pH 7.37 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 56 mm Hg (35 to 45), PaO2 58 mm Hg (75 to 100), and HCO3- 32 mEq/L (22 to 28). Hemoglobin is 17.0 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0). Polysomnography shows 42 apneas and hypopneas per hour with continued chest and abdominal effort during the events. Echocardiography estimates a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 54 mm Hg (15 to 30). The diagnosis is obesity hypoventilation syndrome with obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings establishes that she has obesity hypoventilation syndrome in addition to obstructive sleep apnea?
options: Apnea-hypopnea index above 30 events per hour
Absent respiratory effort during apneas
Awake PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg
Oxygen desaturation during REM sleep
approach: Obstructive sleep apnea is defined by events during sleep: airway collapse with continued effort.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires hypercapnia while awake (PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg) in a person with BMI 30 or more, with other causes excluded.
Her awake PaCO2 of 56 with a raised bicarbonate shows chronic daytime hypoventilation.
questions.why: In obstructive sleep apnea, the pharynx collapses during sleep while the chest and diaphragm keep trying to breathe, causing snoring, arousals, and daytime sleepiness. Central sleep apnea shows pauses with no respiratory effort, as in heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes breathing) or opioid use. In obesity hypoventilation, a heavy chest wall and abdomen reduce compliance and increase the work of breathing, and the drive to breathe adapts to a higher CO2. Chronic hypoxemia causes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (her leg edema), and stimulates erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia. Her high bicarbonate is the renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis.
whyNot: An apnea-hypopnea index above 30 per hour grades obstructive sleep apnea as severe. It says nothing about daytime ventilation.
Absent respiratory effort during apneas defines central sleep apnea. She has continued effort.
Correct.
Desaturation during REM sleep is common in sleep apnea and other lung diseases. It does not show daytime hypoventilation.

questions.stem: During an obstructive apnea, her PaO2 falls from 58 to 42 mm Hg while her PaCO2 rises. Which of the following best describes how her chemoreceptors respond?
options: Carotid body firing rises steeply below a PaO2 of 60 mm Hg
Medullary chemoreceptors sense the fall in PaO2 directly
Medullary chemoreceptors sense arterial H+ crossing into CSF
Carotid bodies respond only after PaO2 falls below 30 mm Hg
approach: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are the only receptors that sense hypoxemia.
Their response is small at normal PaO2 and rises steeply once PaO2 drops below about 60 mm Hg.
Central chemoreceptors respond to CO2, which crosses the blood-brain barrier and forms H+ in the CSF.
questions.why: Central chemoreceptors near the ventral surface of the medulla respond to changes in CSF H+. CO2 diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier and is hydrated to carbonic acid, but arterial H+ and HCO3- cross slowly. A rise in PaCO2 therefore stimulates breathing strongly within minutes. The carotid bodies, through the glossopharyngeal nerve, respond to low PaO2, high PaCO2, and low pH, and they mediate nearly all of the hypoxic drive. Their firing climbs sharply below a PaO2 of about 60 mm Hg, matching the steep part of the oxygen dissociation curve. Each apnea ends when rising chemical drive and arousal reopen the airway.
whyNot: Correct.
Central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen. Hypoxemia is detected only by the peripheral chemoreceptors.
Arterial H+ crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly. CO2 is what crosses and lowers CSF pH.
The carotid body response begins well above 30 mm Hg and increases sharply once PaO2 falls below about 60 mm Hg.

topics: Ventilatory response to hypoxemia and hypercapnia

questions.stem: Indirect calorimetry shows an oxygen consumption of 300 mL/min and a carbon dioxide production of 255 mL/min. Which of the following correctly gives her respiratory quotient and what it indicates?
options: 0.70, oxidation of mainly fat
0.85, oxidation of a mixed fuel supply
1.00, oxidation of mainly carbohydrate
1.18, net conversion of carbohydrate to fat
approach: Respiratory quotient = CO2 produced / O2 consumed = 255/300 = 0.85.
Pure carbohydrate gives 1.0, protein about 0.8, and fat about 0.7.
A value of 0.85 means a mix of fuels, and a shift toward carbohydrate would raise CO2 production at the same O2 use.
questions.why: The respiratory quotient reflects the chemistry of each fuel. Glucose oxidation produces one CO2 for each O2 used (RQ 1.0). Fats are more reduced, so they use more O2 for each CO2 made (about 0.7). Protein gives about 0.8. An RQ above 1.0 means net lipogenesis, as with overfeeding of carbohydrate. In a person who cannot easily raise ventilation, such as someone with obesity hypoventilation or COPD, a high-carbohydrate load raises CO2 production and can worsen hypercapnia, because alveolar ventilation must rise in proportion to CO2 production to keep PaCO2 steady.
whyNot: 0.70 would mean mainly fat oxidation, as in prolonged fasting, and needs a lower CO2 output for this O2 use.
Correct.
1.00 would need CO2 production equal to O2 consumption, about 300 mL/min.
1.18 is O2 divided by CO2, the inverse of the correct calculation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the oropharynx is the usual site of airway collapse during her sleep?
options: Its lumen is lined by keratinized epithelium
Its lymphoid tissue swells during each night
Its muscles are supplied by sympathetic fibers
Its walls lack bony or cartilage support
approach: The nasopharynx is held open by bone, and the larynx by cartilage.
The oropharynx, behind the soft palate and tongue, depends on the tone of dilator muscles such as the genioglossus.
Muscle tone falls during sleep, and fat around the airway and a large tongue narrow it further, so the oropharynx collapses.
questions.why: The pharynx has three parts. The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity above the soft palate and holds the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) and the openings of the pharyngotympanic tubes. The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity and holds the palatine tonsils and the lingual tonsil at the base of the tongue. The laryngopharynx lies behind the larynx. Together the pharyngeal, tubal, palatine, and lingual tonsils form Waldeyer ring. In children, enlarged adenoids and tonsils narrow the airway and cause mouth breathing, snoring, and otitis media from tubal blockage. In adults like her, obesity is the main cause of collapse.
whyNot: The oropharynx is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and the lining does not hold the airway open or closed.
Pharyngeal lymphoid tissue does not swell each night. Enlarged tonsils and adenoids are a fixed cause of obstruction, mainly in children.
The pharyngeal dilator muscles are skeletal muscles supplied mainly by the hypoglossal and vagus nerves, not sympathetic fibers.
